rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\gamma=\frac{F}{l}\ (\text{N m}^{-1});\qquad \eta\ \text{in Pa s}\ (1\ \text{poise}=0.1\ \text{Pa s})$$
$$\text{Clausius–Clapeyron: }\ln\frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}=\frac{\Delta H_{\text{vap}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)$$
$$\text{Capillary rise: }h=\frac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Evaporation happens only at the boiling point. ✅ It occurs at every temperature from the liquid surface; boiling is evaporation throughout the bulk at the boiling point.  ·  ❌ Vapour pressure depends on how much liquid is present. ✅ It depends only on the liquid's nature and the temperature (and on the presence of solutes).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Vapour pressure of water: 23.8 mm Hg at 25 °C, 760 mm Hg at 100 °C (normal boiling point).  ·  Surface tension of water ≈ 72 mN m⁻¹ at 25 °C, falling to zero at the critical temperature (374 °C).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Why does a wet cloth dry faster on a windy day? **Solution:** wind removes the vapour layer above the surface, keeping the vapour pressure below saturation so the net evaporation rate stays high; higher temperature and larger exposed area act in the same direction.  ·  **Problem:** Estimate the boiling point of water at 8000 m where the pressure is about 0.36 atm. **Solution:** the boiling temperature is reached when vapour pressure equals 0.36 atm ≈ 274 mm Hg; from vapour-pressure tables this corresponds to about 72 °C — hence cooking takes much longer at altitude.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: liquid state, physical properties of liquids — evaporation, condensation, vapour pressure (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of the liquid state  ·  A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape: molecules are close together (short intermolecular distances) and slide over one another, so a liquid can flow, is practically incompressible and shows short-range order only. Intermolecular forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together but not strong enough to fix them in a lattice, as in a solid.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Viscosity of water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s at 20 °C; glycerol ≈ 1.5 Pa s — about a thousand times greater.  ·  answer pattern for "Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporatio…": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporatio…" with one example.  ·  compare "Liquid state" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Remember the three marks-carrying definitions: vapour pressure (equilibrium), boiling point (vapour pressure = external pressure), surface tension (force per unit length).  ·  For liquids, viscosity *decreases* with temperature, whereas for gases it increases — a standard one-mark comparison.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Evaporation and condensation  ·  **Evaporation** is the escape of high-energy molecules from the *surface* of a liquid into the vapour phase at any temperature below the boiling point. It is endothermic (the liquid cools — earthen pots, sweating, petrichor), and its rate increases with temperature, surface area, wind/movement and dryness of the air, and decreases with humidity.…  ·  ### 3. Vapour pressure and boiling point

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • Boiling point  ·  • Surface tension  ·  ❌ Surface tension makes the surface a real skin. ✅ It is an inward pull on surface molecules that makes the surface behave like a stretched membrane.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Glycerine is more viscous than water because it is denser. ✅ Viscosity comes from stronger intermolecular (H-bonding) attraction, not from density.  ·  ❌ A liquid boils when the vapour pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure. ✅ Boiling starts when vapour pressure *equals* the external pressure (an overshoot just makes it boil faster).  ·  Syllabus asks for qualitative treatment only: describe causes, trends and applications, not derivations.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Distinguish between evaporation and boiling.  ·  Explain why water boils below 100 °C on a mountain and above 100 °C in a pressure cooker.  ·  State the limitations of the simple description of liquid properties.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: one worked example for "Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporatio…" — check units / edge cases.  ·  recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour when it is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature. It depends only on the nature of the liquid and the temperature — **not** on the amount of liquid or the size of the container.…  ·  **Boiling** occurs when the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure; the temperature at that point is the boiling point, and heat supplied thereafter goes into converting liquid to vapour (latent heat of vaporisation) so the temperature stays constant.…  ·  ### 4.
